Testimony in Support of LD 1800 Submitted by Adam Saltz, DMD, MS, MPH
Chairpersons and Members of the Committee:
My name is Adam Saltz. I am a board-certified periodontist practicing in South Portland, Maine. I currently serve as President of the Maine Dental Association and Vice Chair-Elect to the American Dental Association's New Dentist Committee. I thank you for the opportunity to testify in strong support of LD 1800.
This bill addresses an unfair and growing practice among some dental insurers that require dentists to adhere to capped fees for services that are not even covered by the patient's plan. In other words, dental plans are dictating prices for procedures they refuse to pay for. This practice undermines the provider-patient relationship and threatens the financial viability of dental practices across our state, particularly those in rural or underserved areas.
When an insurer attempts to set fees for services it does not cover, it interferes not only with the clinical autonomy of the provider but also with the transparency we owe to our patients. Patients should know when their insurance covers a procedure and when it does not. They should also understand that services not covered by their plan are not subject to price controls by the insurer. This bill ensures that fees for non-covered services are established fairly, through mutual understanding between the patient and the provider, rather than dictated unilaterally by third parties with no clinical role in care delivery.
Moreover, LD 1800 strengthens patient protection by reinforcing the distinction between covered and non-covered services. It also upholds professional integrity by preventing outside entities from coercing providers into financial arrangements that compromise the sustainability of quality dental care.
I urge the Committee to support this bill and help restore a more balanced, ethical framework for dental care delivery in Maine. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Respectfully,
Adam Saltz, DMD, MS, MPH President, Maine Dental Association

Testimony ofRep. Anne-Marie Mastraccio presenting
LD 1800, An Act to Prohibit Health Care Entities from Requiring
Dentists to Charge Fees for Uncovered Services
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services

Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson and fellow members of the Joint Standing Connnittee
on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services, I am Anne-Marie Mastraccio and I
represent House District 142, which includes part of the City of Sanford and part of the Village
of Springvale. I am here today to present LD 1800, An Act to Prohibit Health Care Entities
from Requiring Dentists to Charge Fees for Uncovered Services.

I submitted this legislation at the request of the Maine Dental Association. This bill would
prohibit insurers, health care service contractors, HMOS and other similar entities from requiring
dentists and other dental professionals to provide, at a set fee, dental care services that are not services covered in a plan. The bill also prohibits third-party administrators from making available to customers a dental plan that sets a fee for a service by a dental care provider in the administrator's network that is not a covered service under the plan.
Most dental insurance plans are defined benefit plans which means there is a maximum benefit
amount paid out on the patient's behalf per year. I have seen a decline in dental providers
agreeing to participate in these plans, making it even more difficult for my constituents to find a
dental home that will also accept and bill their dental insurance.

Thank you for your consideration of this bill. I suggest you save your questions for those
following me as to what brought about this proposal and how it's passage might improve access
to dental care in our state.

District 142: Sanford (part) and Springvale (part)

Re: Support for LD1800 from ME Academy of General Dentistry
To the Members of the Maine Legislature Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services,
I am writing in strong support of LD 1800 (An Act to Prohibit Fee-Setting for Non-Covered Dental Services). This bill represents an essential step forward in protecting both Maine's dental professionals and the patients they serve.
Currently, many insurance contracts allow third-party payers to dictate fees for dental services that are not even covered by the patient's insurance plan. This is not only unjust, it's anticompetitive and harmful to high-quality patient care. Dentists in Maine are being handcuffed by fee-setting mechanisms imposed by insurance companies for services that patients must pay for out of pocket anyway. This leaves providers with two unacceptable choices: deliver the service at a financial loss, or deny the service altogether. Neither serves the public, and both erode the sustainability of comprehensive, patient-centered dental care in our state.
As a practicing dentist, I can attest that the time, training, and clinical nuance required to deliver services in areas like temporomandibular disorders (TMD), sleep-disordered breathing, and advanced restorative care are often significant. Yet, under current policy, providers are forced to accept artificially low fees dictated by insurance companies, even when those services receive no reimbursement from the plan. This directly undermines clinical autonomy and makes it harder for patients to access modern, specialty-level dental care, especially in rural parts of Maine where provider options are already limited.
No other profession is expected to provide services under contractually capped fees when no benefit is being paid. Dentists should not be an exception.
This bill simply ensures that providers retain the right to set fees for non-covered services, not to exploit patients, but to ensure that care can be delivered ethically, sustainably, and in alignment with each patient's unique needs. It also promotes transparency: patients know when a service is not covered, and they can work directly with their provider to understand the cost and value of care.
I respectfully urge the committee to support LD 1800. Let's end these unfair contracting practices and protect access to high-quality dental care for all Mainers.
Sincerely,
 Nicholas K. Roy, DMD, MAGD Representing The Maine Academy of General Dentistry Buxton, ME dr_roy@sacoriverdentistry.com

Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson and Distinguished Members of the Health Coverage,
Insurance and Financial Services Committee,
I am Therese Cahill, and I serve as the Executive Director of the Maine Dental Association. The
MDA represents all dentists in Maine and is a statewide association dedicated to promoting
oral health, advancing excellence in dentistry, and building a future that empowers Maine's communities with sustainable access to oral healthcare. Thank you to Representative
Mastraccio for sponsoring this bill and to all of you for the opportunity to testify today.
On behalf of the Maine Dental Association, I am respectfully providing testimony in support of LD 1800 An Act to Prohibit Health Care Entities Providing Dental Plans from Requiring Dentists
to Charge Fees for Uncovered Services.
It is in Maine's residents' best interest for dental providers to accept dental insurances. By engaging in these agreements, dental professionals help provide access to thousands of
Mainers who may otherwise not be able to afford care. While accepting insurances is not
mandatory for dental providers and often means lower reimbursements than their established fees, dental professionals appreciate and understand the importance of this benefit for their
patients. Unfortunately, there are certain practices in which insurance providers are allowed to
engage that negatively impact the small businesses of these dental providers. Even more
unfortunate is because of these types of insurance practices, dental professionals across the state have been making tough decisions as to whether to continue to accept any or all
insurances. Additionally, when prospective dental providers are researching potential states to determine where they will choose to practice, they will often compare what states do to help or harm establishing a practice.
Currently, Maine is one of only seven states which allows a dental insurance company the ability to set fees dental providers must charge for services the dental insurance company does not cover. It is seemingly counterintuitive to think a dental insurance company can dictate this; they don't cover the service, yet they are able to determine what an independent practitioner
can charge. This bill seeks to correct this practice of overreach.

Senator Bailey, Representative Matheson, and distinguished members of the HCIFS Committee,
My name is Traci Dempsey, I reside in Bath, Maine and am President of the Maine Dental Hygienists' Association representing nearly 1300 dental hygienists in Maine. This testimony is in support of LD1800.
Currently, many dental insurance contracts include "non-covered service fee clauses" with provisions that allow insurers to dictate the maximum allowable fee a dentist can charge for services that the insurer does not even pay for. In other words, they set the price for procedures they have no financial obligation to cover.
This practice is fundamentally unfair. It allows insurers to exert control over the provider-patient relationship and limits a dentist's ability to determine reasonable fees for services based on the actual time, materials, and expertise involved, particularly for elective or specialized treatments.
What this bill does is straightforward and reasonable. It prohibits insurers and dental plans from requiring dentists to accept a set fee for non-covered services. It also prevents third-party administrators from offering dental plans that impose such fee-setting practices on network providers.
These protections are essential for preserving provider independence, promoting transparency in billing, and ensuring patients understand what their insurance does and does not cover. When insurers are allowed to set arbitrary caps on services they don't pay for, it creates confusion for patients and economic pressure on dental practices, especially smaller or rural offices operating with limited resources.
Providers should be able to set their own fees for services not covered by an insurance plan, just as any other business would for services outside of a contract. Patients still have the right to discuss costs, compare providers, and make informed choices, but those choices should not be distorted by insurer overreach.
Dozens of states have already adopted similar laws, recognizing that non-covered service fee caps undermine fair market practices and restrict access to care. It's time for our state to do the same.
I respectfully urge you to vote OTP on LD1800 to protect dental providers and ensure a fair, competitive, and transparent healthcare system for all.
Thank you,
Traci L. Dempsey, RDH, IPDH President, Maine Dental Hygienists' Association Resident of Bath, ME
